en.title: Around 80% of Star Wars Zero Company studio Bit Reactor was reportedly furloughed weeks before its release
en.description: Staff don’t know if they’ll all get their jobs back again, it’s claimed
en.fullContent:
Staff don’t know if they’ll all get their jobs back again, it’s claimed

The majority of staff at Star Wars Zero Company studio Bit Reactor were reportedly furloughed weeks before the game’s release.

Star Wars Zero Company was released last week to widespread critical acclaim, with a Metacritic score currently sitting at 85.

By the time the game had launched, however, most of its developers had reportedly been sidelined without pay as the studio started running out of money.

According to a source speaking to Game File, around 80% of the team has been furloughed, meaning they retain their employee status but have been removed from the company’s active payroll.

Another source told the publication that only a skeleton staff currently remains at Bit Reactor, ready to respond to bug reports following the game’s release on August 27.

en.title: There Is No Greater Joy In Video Games Than Laying Down Some Overwatch And Watching An Absolute Fool Walk Straight Into It
en.description: I have been playing a lot of Star Wars Zero Company this week, and for all the things it does very well--most of which we'll probably get to over t...
en.fullContent:
I have been playing a lot of Star Wars Zero Company this week, and for all the things it does very well--most of which we'll probably get to over the next week or two--there's only one thing that is so good it made me literally hoot out loud at my computer screen.

That thing, as XCOM lovers will have worked out already from the headline, is Overwatch. If you've never played those games (or any of the many other tactics games that use a similar system with a similar name), Overwatch is where you sacrifice a small amount of your current turn's action points in order to direct a unit to cover a certain part of the map with their gun, and if an enemy unit enters that part of the map (usually depicted as a cone of vision) during their turn then your unit will shoot at it.

"But why not just shoot at it in your turn?" someone who hasn't played any of these games might be asking, to which I'll say, "Great question! Here's why". You see, in turn-based tactics games, cover is usually a big deal. If you shoot at an enemy unit while they're hunkered down behind some crates, or around a corner and out of sight, you're wasting your turn (and some bullets) on a target you're very unlikely to hit.

If you wait until you can catch them moving during their turn, though, you've got them dead to rights. An enemy unit running across an Overwatch cone has their weapon down, their gaze focused elsewhere and are usually completely out of cover. They're like First World War soldiers trying to cross No Man's Land, they're like lambs being led to slaughter, they're like rubes getting shot to hell because they walked directly into my trap.

Overwatch rules because while nothing has materially changed in terms of outcome of a battle if you use it--you've shot at and killed some enemies, same as you would have otherwise--the way it's packaged makes you feel like the smartest guy in the room. Like someone who would say in a very whiny voice "You fool, you idiots, you had perfectly good cover! Now you've met your end because of my devious plan!"

Zero Company also very smartly continues the XCOM tradition of telling the player that when enemy reinforcements are on the way, they will be coming from this exact spot on the map, and so if you as the player decide to setup multiple overlapping Overwatch fields across that spawnpoint, and a group of enemies show up and the first thing they do is walk into a hail of blaster fire that makes you jump up and down in your seat clapping, then that's just a thing that's going to happen in this video game. A lot.

en.title: Gems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026
en.description: There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine ...
en.fullContent:
There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
  See all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations here

After 20 years away, Capcom’s hyper kinetic action adventure returns, pitting skilled samurai Miyamoto Musashi against hordes of warriors and demons in Edo-period Kyoto. Master the complex combat then prepare for flashing blades, disembodied limbs and geysers of spraying blood.
  4 September; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox

Billed as the first ever 5D platformer, Screenbound has you navigating a 3D landscape while simultaneously playing an on-screen handheld console, which contains a 2D mirror world. Everything you do in one affects the other in mind-bending ways. The most ingenious puzzle game we’ve seen in a long time.
  10 September; PC, PS5, Xbox

The team behind the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man titles is back with a very different kind of hero. The open-world New York setting is gone in favour of a globe-trotting narrative following Logan on his quest to protect vulnerable mutants. The visuals are gorgeous, while the slick combat brings literal meaning to the term bleeding edge.
  15 September; PS5

The tactical role-playing adventure series returns to the realm explored in the acclaimed Fire Emblem: Three Houses. This time, hopeful contestants arrive at the glorious city of Dagsion to compete in a contest where the winner is granted a single wish. Deep combat, lush settings and fraught relationships are guaranteed.
   17 September; Switch 2

Silent Hill comes to the east coast of Scotland in a beautifully gloomy new horror adventure. You play as Simon Ordell, returning to a quiet harbour town with no memory of whatever catastrophe has taken place there. The place seems abandoned, but you are not alone for long …
  24 September; PC, PS5

en.title: 'Orbitals' is a co-op sci-fi adventure that recaptures the magic of Saturday morning cartoons
en.description: We buddied up to check out Orbitals, a sci-fi anime spin on "It Takes Two"'s classic co-op action.
en.fullContent:
We buddied up to check out Orbitals, a sci-fi anime spin on "It Takes Two"'s classic co-op action.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Growing up, the best Saturday morning cartoons were the ones we re-enacted with our friends on the playground. Whether it was screaming at the top of our lungs to go Super Saiyan like in Dragon Ball Z, or sleuthing around the school as Darkwing Duck.

In the years since our childhood, we’ve often bonded with both strangers and friends over memories of Saturday morning cartoons, remembering the quaint stories and characters that influenced our lives in surprisingly profound ways.

Those stories have a unifying power, and that’s at the heart of developer Shapefarm’s debut, Orbitals, which seeks to combine that rich heart with the gameplay style of Hazelight Studios’ co-op games like It Takes Two and Split Fiction. Will Orbitals be looked back on quite as fondly as those cartoons years down the road? Probably not, but this Switch 2 exclusive is a no-frills co-op smorgasbord that’s delightful from start to finish.

Editor's Note: Since Orbitals requires two players to complete, this feature is co-authored by George Yang and Hayes Madsen. Name a more iconic duo.

en.title: 'More than just a cameo': New Wolverine video game features Squamish language, B.C. sites | CBC News
en.description: A sign featuring the Squamish Nation's language is on display in a new Wolverine video game that’s expected to draw millions of players globally.
en.fullContent:
A sign featuring the Squamish Nation's language is on display in a new Wolverine video game that’s expected to draw millions of players globally.

The game, Marvel’s Wolverine, will be released on Sept. 15 on PlayStation 5 and shows off several slices of B.C., including North Vancouver, the Lions Gate Bridge and the Sea-to-Sky Highway.

At one point, while the main character Logan (aka Wolverine) is driving a motorcycle along the highway, the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim (Squamish language) is displayed on two signs, spelling out the words for Whistler — Sk̲wik̲w — and Squamish — Sḵwx̱wú7mesh.

"It's something that I felt we absolutely had to do," said senior art director Gavin Goulden, who's based in Vancouver. "I worked with the team to get like the proper signage for it."

He said it was also critical to have real parts of Canada represented in the game, since Wolverine's character was born in Alberta.

"Wolverine is a Canadian hero, arguably the most famous Canadian superhero that there is," Goulden said.
